claims.text: A conventional alloy with an appropriate composition and processing history can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition during controlled temperature variation over a narrow temperature window.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys do not exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition associated with temper embrittlement.
The absence of this transition in compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys is due to their inherent resistance to temper embrittlement.
An Fe-Cr-Ni conventional alloy is an example material suitable for producing the proposed transition.
Annealing at 1000°C for 1 hour is an example processing history for the proposed conventional alloy.
The proposed temperature intervention spans 200–400°C at a rate of 5°C/min.
Mechanical response is to be evaluated by uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
Phosphorus and sulfur impurities segregate to grain boundaries in the proposed conventional alloy.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation results in the formation of brittle phases.
Thermally activated diffusion transports impurities to grain boundaries.
The resulting brittle phases cause a loss of ductility.
At the peak embrittlement temperature, elongation to failure will be reduced by 30% relative to its value at 200°C.
The example baseline elongation to failure at 200°C is 20%.
Failure to observe at least a 20% ductility reduction at the peak embrittlement temperature relative to 200°C would falsify the hypothesis.
